The first thing that hits her is the smell.

Not cordite, not oil, not cafeteria food or the faint ozone of some academy’s barrier fields—just cut grass, hot asphalt, and the dull, recycled breath of big gray buildings. Mutsuki blinks once, pupils narrowing against the bright sky above the tree’s branches, then lowers her gaze to the world around her.

Cars rumble past on the road, lined up in orderly, boring little lanes. People in plain clothes file in and out of a squat office building nearby, clutching bags and cups, staring at glowing rectangles in their hands. No halos. No uniforms. No guns openly slung over shoulders. It’s… aggressively normal.

She sits in the grass with her knees drawn up, skirt puffed around her, silver hair a little mussed from however she landed. One hand still grips the familiar weight of her weapon’s strap, as if she expects someone to shout “Training exercise!” any moment now. No shout comes. Just the distant beeping of a crosswalk signal and the whoosh of an automatic door.

“Huh…” Her lips curl in a small, amused smile that doesn’t quite reach her eyes. “Did Aru seriously drag me into a low-budget simulation as a joke? Kukuku… talk about overcommitting.”

She watches a car stop at a red light with religious obedience. The driver doesn’t even look like he’s afraid of being shot for cutting in line. That’s weirder than anything. Her halo’s faint crimson glow catches in the glass of the building as she tilts her head, studying her own reflection: same outfit, same horns, same dangerous little gremlin grin. At least that much hasn’t changed.

Then she notices you.

You’re the one who’s stopped on the sidewalk, not pretending she’s invisible, not briskly sidestepping the strange girl under the tree. Your eyes linger on her halo, her outfit, the way she clearly does not belong in front of a completely ordinary workplace. You recognize that much, at least; she can see it in the flicker of your expression.

Her smile sharpens, interested.

“Oh?” she drawls, sing-song, lifting a hand in a lazy half-wave. “You can see me, huh? And you’re not running away screaming. That’s… either very brave, or very stupid.”

She pushes herself to her feet in one fluid motion, brushing stray blades of grass from her skirt. Up close, she’s smaller than her aura suggests, but there’s nothing small about the way she looks you over—like she’s cataloguing you, poking at your face with her eyes the way someone else might with a knife.

“This place isn’t any district I know,” she muses aloud, as if you’d asked. “No Gehenna, no Millennium… not even some tacky Trinity knockoff. So…”

She steps closer, just enough to lean into your space, peering up at you with a playful, dangerous glint.

“Why don’t you tell me where I’ve landed, mister–or-miss–‘stares-at-girls-under-trees-during-work-hours’?” Her voice lilts with mocking sweetness. “And don’t lie. I’m in a reaaally curious mood today.”

Her fingers tap a light rhythm on the strap of her weapon, a casual little percussion that promises she’s perfectly willing to turn boredom into chaos if she doesn’t like the answers.
